diagnostic_evidence.quote: Nonreal quaternions \qa,\qb are called similar if there exists a nonzero quaternion \qp such that \qp[][-1]\qa\qp = \qb.
Nonreal quaternions \qa,\qb are similar if and only if \rea = \reb and \Abs{\qa} = \Abs{\qb}.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof applies the similarity notation and the cited characterization to a1+a2 and b1+b2 without ensuring that these sums are nonreal. The hypotheses permit, for example, a1=b1=i and a2=b2=-i, in which case both sums are zero. Thus the invoked definition and lemma do not apply in this degenerate case.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle real or zero sums separately, or derive preservation of Re(a1a2) directly from simultaneous conjugation rather than through similarity of the sums.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of the pairwise-similarity criterion does not cover opposing imaginary parts whose sum is real or zero.
issues.title: Pairwise-similarity proof applies similarity to a possibly real sum
issues.why_classification: A short degenerate-case argument or direct local derivation repairs the proof without changing the stated criterion or any later scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: if and only if \qa[1] \sim \qb[1] and \qa[2] \sim \qb[2] and \Re(\qa[1]\qa[2]) = \Re(\qb[1]\qb[2])

issues.failure_explanation: Equation (2.1) supplies a q that conjugates only the sum a1+a2 to b1+b2. It does not ensure that the same q factors as q=q1q2 with q2 commuting with b1. For example, when a1=b1=i and a2=b2=j, q=(i+j)/sqrt(2) fixes i+j under conjugation and q1=1 maps a1 to b1, but q2=q does not commute with i. The subsequent deduction of the second conjugacy is therefore unsupported.

failure_location.quote: Assume that \qq[1] is a nonzero quaternion with \qq[1][-1]\qa[1]\qq[1]=\qb[1]. Set \qq = \qq[1]\qq[2], where \qq[2] is a nonzero quaternion such that \qb[1]\qq[2] = \qq[2]\qb[1].

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the factorization argument by a proof that equal lengths and the preserved inner product give a common rotation, including separate treatment of linearly dependent and independent imaginary parts.
issues.overall_effect: The converse direction of the pairwise-similarity characterization is not established as written, so inferring simultaneous conjugacy from the three scalar invariants remains unproved.
issues.title: Converse proof assumes an unestablished commuting factorization
issues.why_classification: The statement can be preserved, but the repair requires a contained nontrivial simultaneous-conjugacy argument and case split rather than a purely local correction.

It never proves the converse: that a quaternion satisfying those two transformed equations also maps a2 to b2. That converse requires reconstructing a2 from a1 and a1×a2 using the preserved invariants, with a separate collinear case when the cross product vanishes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let \qa[1],\qa[2],\qb[1],\qb[2] be nonreal quaternions with (\qa[1],\qa[2]) \sim (\qb[1], \qb[2]) and \lambda_1, \lambda_2, and \mu real numbers with \Abs{\lambda_1} + \Abs{\mu_1\,\Im{(\qa[1] + \qb[1])}} \neq 0 and \lambda_2 \neq 0.
such that by Theorem~\ref{theorem:NONZERO_SOLUTIONS_OF_THE_HOMOGENEOUS_SYLVESTER_EQUATION} and for real numbers \lambda_2, \mu_2 with \Abs{\lambda_2} + \Abs{\mu_2\,(\qa[3] + \qb[3])} \neq 0 we obtain

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem does not exclude a1×a2=0. In that case pairwise similarity gives b1×b2=0, so a3=b3=0. The cited Sylvester-solution theorem, which applies to similar nonreal quaternions, is being used outside its hypotheses. Moreover, the displayed formula gives q2=lambda2 sqrt(0)=0 despite lambda2 being nonzero, and hence q=q1q2=0. For example, a1=a2=b1=b2=i satisfies the hypotheses and q=1 is a solution, but the formula represents no nonzero solution.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a nonzero-cross-product hypothesis to the displayed q2 branch and separately state that, in the collinear case, the solution set is the solution set of the single Sylvester equation for the first observation.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed general solution fails for collinear pairs: it produces a zero quaternion and omits the actual nonzero zero-cost solutions.
issues.title: Main solution formula degenerates to zero for collinear observations
issues.why_classification: A separate degenerate branch restores the theorem without replacing its overall construction, but the current formula loses an admitted regime and requires more than a typographical fix.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed commutator calculation drops the lambda2 term by implicitly assuming that every chosen square root of a3b3* commutes with b1. That fails when a3=-b3: the radicand is a negative real number and its square roots include many pure quaternions. For instance, with b1=i, a3=j, and b3=-j, k is a square root of -1 and satisfies the stated perpendicularity condition, but ki=-ik, so k does not commute with b1. Such a q2 solves the second Sylvester equation but not the required first commutation equation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the a3=-b3 branch, impose the missing commutation condition q2b1=b1q2, equivalently restrict the square-root direction to the axis parallel to b1, and prove that restricted branch separately.
issues.overall_effect: In the antipodal case, the theorem's parameter set contains quaternions that are not solutions of Wahba's zero-cost equation, so the stated solution set is too large.
issues.title: Antipodal cross-vector case admits nonsolutions in the parameterization
issues.why_classification: A contained special-case restriction can preserve the main closed-form result, but repairing the false commutator inference requires a new branch rather than a routine local correction.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Wahba's problem aims at finding a nonzero quaternion \qq that minimizes the cost function
In this paper, we solve the Wahba's problem for the special and practically important case \ell = 2.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper defines Wahba's problem as a minimization problem, but its formal results characterize only exact zero-cost solutions under pairwise similarity. When the pairs are not pairwise similar, the paper gives neither the minimum cost nor a minimizing quaternion. Thus claims to solve or completely characterize the Wahba problem exceed the established exact-fit case.

failure_location.quote: The presented results offer a complete theoretical characterisation of the Wahba problem in quaternions

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Qualify the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as solving the zero-cost, pairwise-similar two-observation case, and explicitly state that nonzero-cost minimization is outside the established results.
issues.overall_effect: Readers are led to believe that arbitrary two-observation Wahba instances, including inconsistent or noisy observations, are solved in closed form, whereas only the zero-cost feasible case is addressed.
issues.title: Prose claims a complete Wahba solution beyond the zero-cost case
issues.why_classification: The correction is confined to the paper's stated scope, but it materially narrows the advertised guarantee while leaving the exact-fit contribution intact.
